hints: Focus on where you have seen double and triple bonds before, since every double bond has one pi bond and every triple bond has two.
Think of a familiar example for carbon first, like $\text{C}=\text{C}$ in ethene or $\text{C}=\text{O}$ in carbonyls, to confirm it definitely forms pi bonds.
Now check oxygen and nitrogen the same way by recalling $\text{O}=\text{O}$ and $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$, and see if any of the three are left out.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a pi bond is**

A single bond is one sigma bond. A double bond is one sigma plus one pi. A triple bond is one sigma plus two pi.

So the question is really asking: which elements can form multiple bonds?

**Check carbon**

Carbon forms multiple bonds very easily. Think of ethene, $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$, ethyne, $\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}$, and carbon dioxide, $\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$.

$$\text{C}=\text{C}, \quad \text{C}\equiv\text{C}, \quad \text{C}=\text{O}$$
All contain pi bonds, so 1 is correct.

**Check oxygen and nitrogen**

Oxygen forms a double bond in $\text{O}_2$. That is one sigma plus one pi bond.

$$\text{O}=\text{O}$$
Nitrogen forms a triple bond in $\text{N}_2$. That is one sigma plus two pi bonds.

$$\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$$
So 2 and 3 are also correct.

**Combine the conclusion**

Since carbon, oxygen and nitrogen can all be involved in pi bonds, statements 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

That matches the combination for all three correct.

options.A: Correct. All three elements form pi bonds. Carbon in $\text{C}=\text{C}$, $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ and $\text{C}=\text{O}$, oxygen in $\text{O}=\text{O}$, and nitrogen in $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ and $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$.
options.B: Incorrect. This option includes only 1 and 2. It wrongly leaves out nitrogen, but nitrogen clearly forms two pi bonds in $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$.
options.C: Incorrect. This option includes only 2 and 3. It wrongly leaves out carbon, but carbon is the classic pi bond former in alkenes, alkynes, carbonyls and nitriles.
options.D: Incorrect. This option includes only 1. It wrongly suggests oxygen and nitrogen cannot form pi bonds, confusing pi bonding with something only carbon does.
